name: Modal dialog
explanation: A window that opens on top of the page and blocks interaction with the rest of the page until it is dismissed.
triggers: pop up;dialog box;window on top;confirm box;are you sure
requirements: Close it with the Escape key and a visible close button;Move focus into the dialog when it opens and keep it there while open;Return focus to the element that opened it when it closes;Stop the page behind from scrolling while it is open;Give it role=dialog, aria-modal=true and a label taken from its title;Make the page behind inert, for example with the native dialog element and showModal(), or the inert attribute

name: Backdrop blur / overlay
explanation: A semi-transparent layer behind a dialog that dims or blurs the page underneath, often made with the CSS backdrop-filter property.

requirements: Cover the whole viewport behind the dialog, above all other content;Use a plain semi-transparent colour where backdrop-filter is unsupported;Hide the page behind from screen readers while the dialog is open;Keep the blur light enough to stay smooth on low-end phones

name: Entry and exit transitions
explanation: Animations that play when an element appears or disappears, such as fading or sliding in and out.

requirements: Animate only opacity and transform so it stays smooth;Keep it short, around 150 to 300 milliseconds;Play a matching exit animation before removing the element;Turn motion off or down when the user prefers reduced motion
done_when: Opening and closing look smooth, with no jumps or flicker;With reduced motion enabled, it appears and disappears without sliding

name: Outside-click dismissal
explanation: Closing a dialog, menu or popover when the user clicks or taps anywhere outside it.
triggers: click outside;tap outside;close it when i click;close when i click;close when clicking;click anywhere else;click elsewhere;click somewhere else
requirements: Close only on clicks or taps that start outside the element;Ignore the click on the button that opened it, so it does not reopen at once;Do not close while the user is selecting text that ends outside;Remove the click listener when it closes
done_when: Clicking or tapping anywhere outside closes it;Clicking inside it, including on form fields, keeps it open

name: Focus management

triggers: focus;tab key;keyboard users;cursor jumps;put the cursor;focus the first field;cursor in the first
requirements: Move focus to the first useful element when the component opens;Keep Tab and Shift+Tab cycling inside it while it is open;Return focus to the element that opened it when it closes;Show a clearly visible focus outline

name: Escape-key handling
explanation: Letting users close a dialog, menu or overlay by pressing the Esc key.
triggers: escape;esc key;press esc
requirements: Close only the topmost open layer, such as a menu inside a dialog;Listen for Escape only while the component is open;Return focus to the element that opened it when it closes
done_when: Pressing Escape closes the open dialog, menu or popover;Pressing Escape with nothing open does nothing

name: Keyboard navigation
explanation: Making every interactive element reachable and usable with the keyboard alone, in a logical order.

requirements: Make every interactive element reachable with Tab, in a logical order;Use real buttons and links, or give custom controls tabindex and key handlers;Show a clearly visible focus outline;Use arrow keys inside menus, tabs and lists, and Tab to move between them;Never trap focus, except inside an open dialog
done_when: The whole page can be used without a mouse;You can always see where the keyboard focus is

name: ARIA attributes
explanation: HTML attributes such as role and aria-label that describe elements to screen readers and other assistive technologies.
triggers: screen reader;blind users;assistive technology;read aloud;accessible
requirements: Prefer native HTML elements such as button, a and input over ARIA roles;Give every control an accessible name, from visible text, aria-label or aria-labelledby;Keep states such as aria-expanded, aria-selected and aria-checked in sync with the UI;Hide decorative icons with aria-hidden=true, but never hide focusable elements;Do not add roles that conflict with an element's native meaning;Make the accessible name contain the visible label, ideally at the start

name: Color contrast
explanation: Making sure text and controls stand out enough from their background to be readable, measured against WCAG contrast ratios.
triggers: hard to read;readable;low vision;text is not visible;contrast;colors look faded
requirements: Give normal text a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background;Give large text (24px, or about 19px bold) a contrast ratio of at least 3:1;Give icons, input borders and focus indicators at least 3:1 against nearby colours;Never use colour alone to show meaning, such as errors or required fields;Check contrast in every theme and in hover and focus states (disabled controls are exempt but should stay legible)
done_when: A contrast checker passes all text and controls;Errors and states are still clear in greyscale

name: Reduced motion
explanation: Respecting the user's operating-system setting to minimise animation, using the prefers-reduced-motion media query.
triggers: less animation;motion sickness;turn off animation;too much animation;dizzy
requirements: Wrap non-essential animation in a prefers-reduced-motion media query;Replace sliding, zooming and parallax with a simple fade or no animation;Stop auto-playing animations and videos, or give them a pause control;Keep essential feedback such as loading indicators, just calmer;Never flash more than three times per second

name: Responsive layout
explanation: A layout that adapts to different screen sizes using flexible widths and CSS media queries.
triggers: mobile;on a phone;on my phone;small screen;different screen sizes;on a tablet;works on mobile;resize
requirements: Include the viewport meta tag with width=device-width;Design for small screens first and add layout for larger screens with media queries;Let content reflow into one column at 320px wide without horizontal scrolling;Make touch targets at least 24 by 24 pixels, ideally 44;Use relative units and let text scale up to 200 percent without breaking the layout;Never lock the page to portrait or landscape
done_when: The page works at phone, tablet and desktop widths without horizontal scrolling;Zooming to 200 percent keeps all content readable and usable

name: Sizing and max-width
explanation: Controlling how wide and tall an element is with width, height, max-width and min-height, often in relative units so it adapts to the screen.
triggers: size;bigger;larger;smaller;wider;taller;change the size;too small;too big;full width;full screen;too wide;too narrow;stretches
requirements: Limit text width for reading, around 60 to 80 characters per line;Prefer relative units such as rem, percent and viewport units over fixed pixels;Use min-height rather than a fixed height when content can grow;Set width and height or aspect-ratio on images and videos to avoid layout shift;Use box-sizing: border-box so padding does not change an element's size;Keep content working when users increase line height, letter spacing and word spacing
done_when: Long text and translations never overflow or get cut off;Nothing jumps in size while the page loads

name: CSS Grid and Flexbox
explanation: CSS layout systems for arranging elements in rows, columns and grids, and for aligning and spacing them.
triggers: side by side;center it;centre it;align;columns;in a row;line up;spacing
requirements: Use Flexbox for layouts in one direction and Grid for rows and columns together;Use gap for spacing between items instead of margins on each item;Keep the visual order the same as the HTML order, for keyboard and screen readers;Let items wrap or stack on small screens instead of shrinking until unreadable;Avoid absolute positioning for page layout

name: Dark mode
explanation: An alternative colour scheme with light text on dark backgrounds, often following the system setting via prefers-color-scheme.
synonyms: dark theme;night mode;prefers-color-scheme;night theme;dark colour scheme
triggers: light and dark;theme toggle;switch theme;dark background;darker colors
requirements: Follow the system setting with prefers-color-scheme by default;Let users switch manually and remember their choice;Define colours as CSS variables so both themes stay in sync;Check text contrast in both themes
done_when: The page loads in the right theme without a flash of the wrong one;All text meets contrast guidelines in both themes

name: Toast notification
explanation: A small, temporary message that appears briefly to confirm an action or report a problem without interrupting the user.

requirements: Show it in a corner without covering important content;Hide it after about 4 to 6 seconds, pausing while hovered or focused;Announce it to screen readers with role=status or aria-live;Let users dismiss it, and stack several toasts neatly

name: Loading states and skeleton screens
explanation: Placeholders or spinners shown while content is loading, so the interface feels responsive instead of frozen.

triggers: load later;only when needed;faster page load;load on scroll;page loads slowly;big images;scroll into view;visible on screen;load images;takes forever;slow to load
requirements: Add loading=lazy to images and iframes further down the page, not to the main top image;Reserve space with width and height so content does not jump when it loads;Load heavy components and routes on demand with dynamic import;Show a placeholder or skeleton while lazy content loads;Start loading a little before content scrolls into view
done_when: The first screen loads quickly and its main image is not delayed;Scrolling never shows layout jumps or long-empty gaps

name: Infinite scroll

name: Pagination
explanation: Splitting a long list of results into pages, using page numbers or a cursor that marks where the next page starts.

requirements: Show the current page and links to the previous and next pages;Keep the page number in the URL so pages can be bookmarked;Disable previous on the first page and next on the last;Use cursor-based pagination for large or frequently changing data;Return a next page token or link, and cap the page size

name: Debouncing and throttling
explanation: Limiting how often a function runs, for example waiting until the user stops typing before sending a search request.

requirements: Debounce search as you type, sending a request after a pause of about 200 to 300 ms;Throttle scroll and resize handlers, or use requestAnimationFrame;Ignore or cancel responses to outdated requests so old results never replace new ones;Run the action immediately on Enter or submit, without waiting for the delay

name: Autocomplete
explanation: Suggesting matching options in a dropdown as the user types into an input.
triggers: suggestions;as you type;dropdown suggestions;search box
requirements: Wait until the user pauses typing before searching (debounce);Move through suggestions with the arrow keys and choose with Enter;Close the list with Escape or when focus leaves the input;Use the combobox pattern with aria-expanded and aria-activedescendant;Show a message when nothing matches

name: Form validation
explanation: Checking user input before it is accepted and showing clear error messages next to the fields that need fixing.
triggers: validate;required field;error message;invalid email;form errors;check the input;wrong format;error under;field is wrong;field is invalid;email field
requirements: Show each error next to its field in plain words;Validate when the user leaves a field or submits, not on every keystroke;Keep everything the user typed when showing errors;Link errors to fields with aria-describedby and focus the first error on submit;Validate again on the server;Set aria-invalid=true on fields with errors;Suggest how to fix each error, such as the expected format
done_when: Submitting invalid data shows clear messages and sends nothing;Screen readers read the error for each field;Valid data submits successfully

name: Drag and drop
explanation: Letting users move items by pressing, dragging and releasing them, for example to reorder a list or upload files.
triggers: drag;reorder;drop files;move items around;rearrange
requirements: Offer a way to do the same without dragging, such as move up and move down buttons;Support reordering with the keyboard, such as picking up with Space and moving with arrows;Show where the item will land while it is dragged;Announce the result to screen readers with an aria-live region;Support touch as well as mouse, using pointer events

name: Feature flags
explanation: Switches in code or configuration that turn a feature on or off without deploying new code.
triggers: release a feature;turn on a feature;turn off a feature;hide a feature;enable a feature;disable a feature;kill switch;without deploying;without a deploy;toggle a feature
requirements: Give every flag a clear name, an owner and a planned removal date;Fall back to the safe value when the flag service cannot be reached;Decide flags on the server for anything security or billing related;Test the code with the flag both on and off;Remove the flag and the old code path once the rollout is complete
done_when: Turning the flag off restores the old behaviour without a deploy;No flag is older than its planned removal date

name: Percentage rollout
explanation: Enabling a feature for a chosen share of users, such as 10%, and increasing that share over time.
triggers: % of users;percent of users;portion of users;fraction of users;small group of users;some of the users
requirements: Assign users by hashing a stable user id, so each user always gets the same version;Start small, such as 1 to 5 percent, and increase in steps;Check error rates and key metrics at each step before increasing;Keep a one-step way to drop back to 0 percent
done_when: The same user sees the same version on every visit and device;Metrics for the new version are compared with the old before going to 100 percent

name: Feature targeting
explanation: Choosing which users see a feature using rules such as country, plan, account or user group.
triggers: of users;specific users;certain users;beta users;premium users;user group;only for admins;show the beta;by country;certain customers;customers in
requirements: Evaluate targeting rules on the server, not only in the browser;Base rules on stable details such as account id, plan or country;Record which rule decided each result, so behaviour can be explained;Give a sensible default for users who match no rule

explanation: Releasing a change to production in steps instead of all at once, watching for problems before continuing.
triggers: release;roll out;gradually;little by little;not all at once
requirements: Roll out in stages, such as one server group or region at a time;Define health checks and error limits that must pass before the next stage;Pause or roll back automatically when the limits are crossed;Keep old and new versions compatible with the same database and APIs meanwhile
done_when: A bad release reaches only the first stage before it is stopped;Each stage completes only after its health checks pass

explanation: Sending a small share of real traffic to a new version first, so problems show up before everyone is affected.
triggers: test in production;few servers;try it on a few users first;early warning
requirements: Send a small share of traffic, such as 1 to 5 percent, to the new version first;Compare its error rate, speed and key metrics with the current version;Promote it only when its metrics are as good as the current version's;Route each user consistently, so one user does not switch between versions

explanation: Returning a system to its previous working version after a bad release.
triggers: undo the deploy;go back;previous version;broke production;revert;bad deploy
requirements: Keep the previous release ready to deploy in one step;Make database migrations backward compatible, so the old code still works after them;Practise the rollback procedure before you need it;Record what was rolled back and why
done_when: Rolling back takes minutes and needs no code changes;The previous version works with the current database

name: A/B testing
explanation: Showing different versions of a feature to separate groups of users and measuring which one performs better.

explanation: Automation that builds, tests and deploys code every time changes are pushed.

requirements: Run the build and the tests on every push and pull request;Block merging when the build or the tests fail;Keep secrets in the CI secret store, never in the repository;Deploy the same build that was tested;Keep the pipeline fast, ideally under 10 minutes;Give pipeline tokens the fewest permissions, and review changes to the pipeline itself;Pin third-party CI actions to a commit hash;Never put untrusted PR titles or branch names straight into scripts, or run PR code in pull_request_target

requirements: Test the most important user flows from start to finish;Unit-test logic with edge cases such as empty, very large and invalid input;Make tests independent and repeatable, never relying on order or the real clock;Run the tests automatically in CI on every change;Test what users see and do, not internal details

name: Environment variables and secrets
explanation: Configuration values such as API keys kept outside the code, so they can differ per environment and stay out of version control.

requirements: Keep secrets and per-environment settings out of the code and the repository;Add .env to .gitignore, and commit a .env.example without real values;Check required variables at startup, and stop with a clear message if one is missing;Never send server secrets to the browser or put them in frontend bundles;Use different keys for development, test and production;Use a secrets manager in production, and rotate secrets regularly

name: REST API
explanation: An HTTP interface where clients read and change resources using methods such as GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.

requirements: Use nouns for resources and HTTP methods for actions, such as GET /orders;Return correct status codes, such as 201 created, 400 bad input and 404 not found;Validate every input and return errors in one consistent format;Paginate list endpoints;Version the API, so changes do not break existing clients;Accept only allowed fields when creating or updating records, to prevent mass assignment;Use plural nouns in paths, and POST to a sub-path such as /orders/{id}:cancel for actions that are not CRUD;Never return passwords or stored secrets, and show a new API key only once, when it is created

name: Authentication
explanation: Verifying who a user is, for example with a password, a one-time code or a sign-in provider such as Google.

requirements: Allow long passwords, at least 64 characters, and reject known breached passwords;Give the same error for a wrong username or a wrong password;Limit repeated failed logins per account and per IP address;Send login forms and session cookies only over HTTPS;Offer two-factor authentication;Require at least 8 characters, or 15 when the password is the only factor;Allow password managers and pasting, and never make a memory test or puzzle the only way to sign in;Never require character mixes or regular password changes, and accept spaces and Unicode

explanation: Deciding what a signed-in user is allowed to do, usually through roles or permissions.

requirements: Check permissions on the server for every request, not only by hiding buttons;Deny by default, and give each role only what it needs;Check that the user may access the specific record, not only that they are signed in;Keep permission checks in one shared place instead of copied around;Add automated tests that check each role is refused what it may not do

requirements: Limit requests per user, API key or IP address in a time window;Apply stricter limits to login, sign-up and password reset;Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header;Enforce limits on the server or gateway, shared across all instances;Limit request body size, uploads and expensive queries

explanation: Keeping a copy of data that is slow to fetch or compute, so later requests can be answered faster.

requirements: Decide how fresh each piece of data must be, and set the expiry time to match;Invalidate or update cached data when the original changes;Never cache one user's private data where another user could receive it;Set Cache-Control headers for static files, and put a content hash in their names;Keep working, only slower, when the cache misses or is down;Cache by Cache-Control and real content type, never because a URL ends in .css or .js (cache deception)

explanation: Running slow tasks such as sending emails or generating reports outside the user's request, usually through a queue.

explanation: Versioned scripts that change a database schema step by step, so every environment stays in sync.

requirements: Index columns used in frequent WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY clauses;Check slow queries with EXPLAIN before and after adding an index;Order columns in combined indexes to match how queries filter;Remove unused indexes, because every index slows down writes;Use unique indexes where duplicates must never happen
